No. Redis adds a failure domain, a deploy dependency, and a second source of truth without solving a constraint you have. One writer means no lock arbitration is needed. SQLite already gives you durability and boot-time restore. No cross-host requirement means no shared cache tier is needed.

What already covers the usual reasons for reaching for Redis:

- In-memory state and caching: a GenServer or ETS table in the same BEAM process, with no network hop and no serialization cost.
- Expiry and TTL: ETS plus a periodic sweep, or `:ets.select_delete` on a timestamp column.
- Pub/sub and fan-out: `Phoenix.PubSub` or plain `Registry`, which work in-node today and switch to distributed transparently if you ever add nodes.
- Queues and scheduled work: Oban on the existing SQLite database, keeping one storage system.

Reconsider Redis when at least one of these becomes true: you run more than one node and need shared mutable state, you need a coordination primitive across hosts (leader election, distributed lock, rate limiter), working-set size outgrows the memory you want the BEAM to hold, or you need state to outlive the process while SQLite is the wrong shape for it. Note that the first two are often better answered in Elixir by distributed Erlang, `:global`, or Horde before an external store.
